title: Hedging with futures
objectives: Compute the number of index futures to hedge a portfolio.
body_md:
## Short hedge

A holder of shares fears a fall and **sells** futures. A loss on the portfolio is offset by a gain on the short futures.

## Long hedge

A buyer who will need shares later **buys** futures to fix the price.

## Portfolio hedge using index futures

**Number of contracts = β × Portfolio value ÷ (Futures price × Lot size)**

Example: portfolio ₹1 crore, β = 1.2, Nifty futures 20,000, lot 50. Contracts = 1.2 × 1,00,00,000 ÷ (20,000 × 50) = **12**.

## Imperfect hedges

- **Basis risk:** futures and spot do not move one-for-one.
- **Beta mismatch:** portfolio β differs from the index.
- **Rollover:** contracts expire; rolling costs money.

## Changing portfolio beta

Selling futures lowers beta; buying raises it, without trading the shares.

> **Exam tip:** Hedging reduces risk and also caps the gain.
example: A ₹50 lakh portfolio with β = 1 and Nifty futures notional of ₹10 lakh per lot needs 5 short lots to fully hedge.
say: A hedge protects the downside but also limits the upside.
Basis risk means the hedge is not perfect.

check.q: To hedge a share portfolio against a fall, one should:
Contracts to hedge = β × portfolio value ÷:
check.why: Divide by the notional value of one contract.

o: Spot and futures do not move perfectly together
